query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The unique thermoelastic and stress–strain behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is governed by a coupling between residual dislocation networks (inherited from cold rolling) and internal stresses generated by local thermal expansion mismatches during processing (composite solidification). In this model, regions with higher mismatch induce additional internal stresses that accelerate thermally activated dislocation climb/recovery at high temperatures (leading to dynamic softening), while aging treatments that relax this mismatch preserve the dislocation interaction and work hardening at intermediate temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr alloy cast via conventional methods and subsequently cold rolled, exhibiting dense dislocation bands and a single-phase BCC structure.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: (a) a baseline set processed by standard cold rolling and annealing and (b) a set processed via controlled composite solidification aimed at accentuating local thermal expansion mismatches. In both cases, perform additional aging treatments (600–800 °C) on sub-sets to partially relax mismatch-induced stresses.
generation.conditions: Tests performed in tension and creep from room temperature up to ~1250 °C, with specific attention to aging effects in the 600–800 °C range; in situ diffraction and TEM used to monitor internal strain and dislocation configurations.
generation.structural_mediator: Internal thermal stresses arising from local differences in thermal expansion (due to compositional variations or microstructural heterogeneity) coupled with the pre-existing, cold-work-induced dense dislocation network.
generation.mechanism: Thermal expansion mismatch produces residual internal stresses that, when combined with a high density of dislocations from cold rolling, lower the barrier for dislocation climb and dynamic recovery at high temperatures. This shifts the balance between work hardening (dominant at lower temperatures) and dynamic softening (dominant at elevated temperatures). Aging treatments can modify this balance by reducing the mismatch and stabilizing the dislocation structures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, samples with enhanced thermal expansion mismatch will exhibit a lower yield strength and more pronounced softening (due to accelerated dynamic recovery) in the high-temperature regime, while aging treatments that relax local mismatches will show higher retained strength and a stronger work-hardening response. In contrast, if the mismatch effect is minimized, the traditional dislocation‐mediated work hardening and softening balance becomes more predictable with temperature.
generation.baseline: Standard cold-rolled and annealed HfNbTaTiZr samples without induced composite solidification features.
generation.boundary: Temperature range from ambient to approximately 1250 °C, with the critical behavior spanning from room temperature (where residual dislocations dictate initial strength) to aging temperatures (600–800 °C) and high-temperature creep conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of dislocations (as seen in PMC10453588::web::011::3_results and PMC10453588::web::019::4_discussion) and the effects of aging (PMC7514597::web::017::4_discussion) have been documented separately, it remains uncertain how thermal expansion mismatch (suggested by issues raised in composite solidification studies like PMC11203300::web::021::4_conclusions) interacts quantitatively with these factors. The novel aspect is extending the interaction between internal thermal stresses from mismatch and dislocation-mediated deformation—a gap not directly addressed previously.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one using standard cold rolling/annealing (baseline) and a second group processed with a controlled composite solidification route designed to enhance local thermal expansion mismatch. Both groups undergo identical aging treatments. Using in situ neutron diffraction and TEM, quantify internal residual stress fields and dislocation configurations. Then, perform tensile and creep tests across the 293–1250 °C range to measure stress–strain responses.
measurements: Internal strain and lattice parameter variation (via in situ ND)
Yield strength, work hardening rate, and creep rate at various temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples processed to enhance thermal expansion mismatch do not show a statistically significant reduction in yield strength and an increased rate of dynamic recovery (i.e. more pronounced softening and altered dislocation configurations) at high temperatures relative to the baseline, then the proposed coupling mechanism between thermal mismatch-induced stresses and dislocation behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The tensile stress–strain curves of the NbTaTiZrV0.5 RHEA at room temperature (RT) and high temperature (673–1273 K) are presented in Figure 4a. The tensile properties of this HEA were shown to be in agreement with a previous study []. At room temperature, the cold-rolled alloy showed excellent tensile properties, with a yield strength approaching 1200 MPa and a plasticity reaching 8%. When the temperature reached 673 K, the strain–stress curve revealed a serrated flow behavior at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1, while the strength decreased, and the plasticity increased greatly. This occurred mainly in the softening phase, which may be related to the reason for the improvement in the plasticity []. When the temperature increased further, the yield strength and plasticity of the alloy decreased stably, but the decreasing range was small. The yield strength decreased significantly, and the plasticity rose to more than 30% when the temperature increased to 1223 K.

Figure 9 shows the true stress–strain curves of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA at different deformation strain rates and temperatures. It was found that all curves had similar trends. That is, with the rise of the strain, the flow stress increased to the peak stress first and then decreased as the strain continued to increase. Before it reached the peak stress, the flow stress rose along with the strain. At this stage, the dislocation density increased due to deformation, the dislocation accumulation increased the deformation resistance, and a work hardening was the main rheological feature. When the flow stress achieved its maximal stress, it steadily declined as the strain increased. This is attributed to the dynamic recovery or dynamic recrystallization softening mechanism in the material exceeding the work-hardening mechanism, which is macrographically manifested as a gradual reduction in the flow stress []. In fact, the process of thermal deformation of materials is a competitive process of work-hardening and softening mechanisms, and the effects of hardening and softening reach an equilibrium when the flow stress reaches the peak stress []. Two model BCC RHEAs, brittle VNbMoTaW and ductile TiZrNbHfTa, were investigated to better understand fundamental aspects of their mechanical behavior. Bulk and micropillar compression tests as a function of temperature and strain rate show the latter is plastically deformable in compression down to 77 K, but the former is not below room temperature. From our experimentally determined enthalpies of compression, the BDTT of VNbMoTaW is estimated to be 627 K (above room temperature) whereas that of TiZrNbHfTa is estimated to be 247 K (below room temperature) which indicates that high dislocation mobility at room temperature is one reason for the latter’s more ductile behavior. Consistent with this, deformation enthalpies and strength models both show kink migration is the rate-controlling step at room temperature in VNbTaMoW but not in TiZrNbHfTa. Another reason for the greater malleability of TiZrNbHfTa is the extremely low energy of screw dislocation cores in this RHEA compared with those in VNbMoTaW. Formation of the single BCC solid solution and the mechanical properties of the homogenization-treated NbTaTiV HEA at elevated temperatures The microstructure of the homogenized NbTaTiV refractory HEA was characterized, using the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) backscattered electron (BSE) technique, as shown in Fig. 1A. A typical simple solid-solution HEA microstructure with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm was identified without the presence of secondary phases or elemental segregations. The chemical composition of the sample was verified (using the point energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy analysis) to be Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8, indicating a homogeneous elemental distribution in a nearly equiatomic percentage. The measured ND patterns of the bulk samples, as illustrated in Fig. 1B, confirm the single BCC solid solution at RT and elevated temperatures. The lattice parameters of the present alloy at RT, 500°, 700°, and 900°C, which were determined by a single-peak fitting approach (), are 3.2318, 3.2445, 3.2511, and 3.2588 Å, respectively. It is not clear whether presence of BCC phases in our less ductile alloys is due to stabilizing by rapid cooling during vacuum arc melting or due to differences between binary alloy and 3, 4 or 5 element alloys. Existence of two BCC phases was reported in similar RHEA system with Mo and V instead of Ta and Nb []. CALPHAD simulation of the HfNbTaTiZr was performed, too []. A mixture of BCC and HCP phases with Ta Zr segregation was predicted. Experimental observation was performed on cold deformed and heat treated alloy in combination with high pressure torsion (HPT) and isothermal annealing in the range 300 °C–1100 °C and BCC + HCP phases were identified. Combination of two BCC phases and HCP was detected in a HfNbTaTiZr specimen annealed at 500 °C for 100 h. On contrary we observed only a single BCC phase in as-cast state. System HfNbTaTi, similar to our NbTaTiZr alloy was calculated by CAPLHAD method []. Also combination of BCC + HCP phases was found to be stable at room temperature the BCC2 phase appeared between 750 °C and 1000 °C.
